items.title: Meta’s AI could still scrape news sites, legal experts say
items.summary: Meta has tweaked its business terms to remove language suggesting that it could freely train its AI models on news sites, like The Verge - but legal experts say these changes aren't enough to address their concerns. "This does nothing to restrict the 'associated with your product
items.content:
Meta’s new business terms could still help it justify training AI on scraped sites.

Meta has tweaked its business terms to remove language suggesting that it could freely train its AI models on news sites, like The Verge — but legal experts say these changes aren’t enough to address their concerns. “This does nothing to restrict the ‘associated with your products or services’ [language] that would let Meta scrape entire sites,” James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell Law School, tells Nieman Lab .

Initially, Meta’s new terms for business accounts appeared to give the company permission to train its AI on news sites. The terms, which go into effect October 30th, stated that Meta “may use any content” from the websites associated with a business account to “develop, research” and “train” Meta’s products. At the time, legal experts told Nieman Lab that this could allow Meta “to argue its commercial terms supersede other blocking instructions,” such as the robots.txt file that has historically told scrapers (including search engines like Google) what they are allowed to crawl.

Following fierce backlash from the publishing industry, Meta removed language saying it would “train” its products with scraped content. But the tweaks might not be enough to rule out that possibility. “The revised version of the new terms still allows Meta to use that scraped content to develop any ‘business product.’ That doesn’t seem to be a defined term, and presumably Meta is developing AI business products. I think ‘develop’ is broad enough to include ‘train,’” Matt Topic, a media and intellectual property attorney at Loevy & Loevy, tells Nieman Lab.

Meta has maintained that its new terms aren’t designed to scrape news content for free. In a statement to The Verge today, Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts reiterated that “content owners can use robots.txt to signal their preferences,” adding that the update “is not about scraping news sites, and these updates don’t give us new rights that supersede those preferences.”

items.title: Meta turns Muse sharing back on
items.summary: Meta has re-enabled Muse sharing after security researchers had reported that public conversation links could be easy to find. The researchers said they had been able to find Muse pages like a marketing company's internal revenue review and a small business owner's loan applicati
items.content:
Meta has given new URLs to shared Muse ‘artifacts’ after security researchers reported that public links could be easy to find.

Meta has re-enabled Muse sharing after security researchers had reported that public conversation links could be easy to find. The researchers said they had been able to find Muse pages like a marketing company’s internal revenue review and a small business owner’s loan application.

Researchers at Claroc reported earlier this week that Muse the web addresses for shared conversations from Muse were named after a conversation’s title and written into public DNS. Ars Technica said Tuesday that Meta paused the sharing feature after it reached out about what was going on.

In a post today on X, Meta’s David Singleton says that “The underlying issue is now fixed, and sharing is back on.” According to Singleton, the issue was with URLs for shared Muse artifacts, which Meta says are things like documents and images inside Muse, and wasn’t a flaw with chat sharing.

“If you shared an artifact before the fix: it now has a new URL,” Singleton says. “Anyone visiting the old link will see a note asking them to get the new one from you. We know that’s a pain, and we’re sorry for the disruption — but protecting user data has to come first.”

items.title: The FCC is beginning to block gadgets with ‘foreign surveillance chips’
items.summary: On October 13th, Brendan Carr's FCC gave itself a new power - it can block gadgets for containing any computer chip made by any company on its list of potential threats to national security. Today, it's exercising that power for the first time, blocking two gadgets because they c
items.content:
The first exercise of a new FCC power.

On October 13th, Brendan Carr’s FCC gave itself a new power — it can block gadgets for containing any computer chip made by any company on its list of potential threats to national security . Today, it’s exercising that power for the first time, blocking two gadgets because they contain “foreign surveillance chips,” the FCC claims .

The agency doesn’t say which specific gadgets it blocked, and it didn’t immediately respond to our request for comment, but it does name the “surveillance chip”: it’s a HiVision Hi3516CV610 UHD Smart Vision SoC , a chip that turns a raw camera sensor into a home security camera, a dashcam, or the like. It’s often sold as a package with a Sony camera sensor and sometimes even a lens already on board, according to listings we viewed on AliExpress.

The FCC is calling it a foreign surveillance chip because HiVision advertises it as “designed for the surveillance market” with “[b]uilt in detection algorithms for human faces,” the FCC explains — and because HiVision is a subsidiary of Huawei, one of the first telecom companies the US government decided to call a national security risk .

Huawei is indeed on the FCC’s Covered List, and the FCC’s new power helps it close a loophole where companies could sneak in banned companies’ products inside another company’s gadgets. It did something similar when it gave itself the power to retroactively ban gadgets , and when it gave itself the power to block modular radio transmitters.

As with the router ban and the Roomba ban , he question remains: is the FCC keeping people safer, or just picking winners and losers while making a show of enforcement ? We’ve asked the agency many times to chat about its efforts, but it won’t engage.

items.title: The Google Home Speaker Has Been Secretly Eating My Wi-Fi Data
items.summary: My Google Home Speaker had been burning through more data than all the rest of my devices combined. As I looked into it further, I found other smart home devices that had the same problem.
items.content:
If you had to estimate how much data your smart speaker was using over the course of a couple of weeks, would you guess three terabytes? That's what one Google Home Speaker user discovered when he checked his home Wi-Fi's usage, according to Reddit posts reported on by 9to5Google . The Google Gemini-powered smart speakers have apparently been downloading huge amounts of data to the device over the past two weeks, which could put a serious damper on your Wi-Fi network.

While it isn't happening to everyone, after checking my own home internet usage, I found out that I have been experiencing the same issue. My Google Home Speaker has used 487 GB of data in the last ten days, using almost as much as the entire rest of my home between August and September.

Google confirmed this bug has only affected some devices, and that they've rolled out a solution. A spokesperson from Google told WIRED: “A server misconfiguration caused some Google Home Speakers to repeatedly download a software update. This issue has now been resolved.”

Looking into this issue made me go beyond just Google's usage, though. My husband and I started reviewing the data usage for all of the individual devices that our router could identify and found some surprising numbers. The weirdest highlight was that Amazon was listed as using 22 GB in the last week with only the Ring smoke detector set up in my house, which was similar to the use of one of the smartphones in my house. There's also a mysterious device just labeled “WATCH” that used about 21 GB in the last week, but no one in my home has a smart watch that's been on in the last year. A mystery for me to solve another day.

If you've noticed your home Wi-Fi bandwidth isn't what it used to be, it could be because one of your smart home devices (or possibly something else entirely). Here's how to check your router or Wi-Fi provider for what device could be at fault.

You have a couple of different options for checking how much data a smart home device has been using. Some routers provide detailed information about where all your data is going, for starters. I have an Eero mesh system for my house, but we don't pay for its subscription fee to access detailed information—so it's fairly limited. The free version of the app still lists all the connected devices in my home, but it doesn't tell me how much data each uses.

There are a lot of routers that have subscription fees and paywalls that can hide this information and other features you might want. But our favorite subscription-free mesh Wi-Fi system comes from Asus, which also makes our favorite regular Wi-Fi router , and you can track and analyze traffic for free with an Asus router. Here's how:

Folks with a TP-Link router or mesh can also review traffic. Here's how:

Netgear only tracks overall traffic under Traffic Meter , you can't break it down by device. For other manufacturers it's worth poking around in the web interface (it usually gives you access to more data than the mobile app). If you're looking to get more information without hitting a paywall, explore both our router and mesh Wi-Fi guides for recommendations.

But even that limited information revealed which devices were gobbling up the most data in the recent days and weeks, which is how we discovered the issue with both the Google Home Speaker and the Ring smoke detector.

It's not a huge issue for me that my Google Home Speaker has been guzzling my data. I have a large Wi-Fi plan (a must as a smart home tester), and it was patched quickly. On the other hand, I have unplugged it for the time being to make sure I don't hit the two terabyte cap we have per billing period. But if you're on a plan where massive downloads like this can cost you, or your signal is getting clogged up by mysterious devices, it might be time to check your data usage to find out which device is at fault. You never know when you'll find a three-terabyte bug slowing down your whole network.

items.title: The Social Society Helping Women Join the AI Boom
items.summary: WIRED spoke with the founders of the Aged Intelligence Society, a fast-growing events startup that brings women together to “solve midlife problems using frontier tools.”
items.content:
I’m not even going to try to pretend I don’t have a bit of a girl-crush on Shoshana Berger. She’s a former WIRED editor turned editorial leader for companies like Notion and Ideo. She’s super smart and chic. And she’s the cofounder, with Nina Willdorf, of the Aged Intelligence Society , a buzzy events startup that hosts invite-only dinner parties where women “solve midlife problems using frontier tools .”

Berger and Willdorf having a refreshingly practical take on AI. “This is the most formative technology of our generation, and it’s here,” Willdorf says. “If you choose to sit it out, you are doing yourself a disservice.”

They also practice what they preach, especially as they juggle kids entering college, their own aging parents, and their increasingly in-demand business. “The midlife cognitive and emotional labor is so heavy and so intense that we need an assistant,” Berger says. “Actually, we need the National Guard, but AI will help in the interim.”

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Zoë Schiffer: How did the Aged Intelligence Society start?

Shoshana Berger: Nina and I are both recovering magazine editors. We ended up at a friend's birthday party, and we were both obsessing over Claude, our new French lover. All the other women had glazed eyes while we were talking; they just weren’t part of the conversation. At some point I said, “Nina, I think this might be a business, because all these women need to be doing what we're doing.”

Nina Willdorf: We were super nervous before the first event …

Berger: We needed to take beta blockers and ashwagandha because we were like, wait, we're inviting all of these baller women, these really smart, incredibly accomplished women, and we’re not AI experts. But we have been doing what we usually did as reporters, which is test the tools in a way many women did not seem to be doing.

There's a million reasons for women to bow out of the conversation, and we were like, “no, no, no, you cannot bow out of this conversation if you are going to be relevant in the work world. You need to be fluent.”

Willdorf: We are not like pom-pom advocates for everything about this, but we feel committed to this idea that being involved is really important.

How do you set up expectations around the event for attendees?

Berger: There are rules of engagement for every party. One is we have an ideological parking lot. So if you want to talk about how AI is going to ruin everything, this is not the best space to do that. There are lots of ways in which we are also terrified about AI and find it can be quite menacing, especially for creatives like us, but that's not what we're here to do. We're here to gain fluency, test things out, and reduce our administrative load.

Willdorf: And eat some really good cheese and drink some wine.

Berger: We have everyone bring a laptop and a midlife problem. We call it a midlife quandary. We spend 15 minutes doing what we call library time. We all bring our laptops out, and you work on your problem. And Nina and I kind of walk around the room sherpa-ing people through the experience: “You might want to try this tool, try this LLM instead. Your prompt is feeling a little weak. You're not getting the answer that you like. Let's work on that and iterate.”

Willdorf: Sometimes people are like, “You know what? I don't really want AI to write for me.” And we're like, “Oh no, no, we don't either. Let us show you a couple other things you can think about.”

You’ve had a wait list for these parties since you started. How do you decide who gets to attend?

Willdorf: We have really found that the optimal number is between like eight and 12. When it gets bigger than that, it's a little bit chaotic. Our best events have been ones where there is a magical mix, and you have somebody that works in nonprofit next to somebody who works in design next to somebody who is home with the kids next to a CEO next to someone who works in philanthropy.

Most people, in my experience, cannot immediately identify a software-shaped problem in their life. How do you help people see an issue that AI could actually help with?

Berger: So much of what we're trying to do is show the pragmatic ways in which it's helping with midlife overload. We're often labeled the sandwich generation. We hate that term because it just sounds like we're the tasteless tomato in between two slabs of bread. But the real part of that is that we are dealing with parents who increasingly need help and kids who maybe are launching, maybe not.

One woman came to an event with a mother who was dealing with an Alzheimer's diagnosis, and she wanted to know whether her mother was qualified for long-term care because she had an insurance plan. Well, the insurance carrier sent her a 300-page packet. Who is going to read through that? This is how insurance companies keep you from using your insurance policy. So of course, she fed it to AI. And the AI came back saying, yes, your mother is absolutely qualified for care, and would you like me to write a letter to the insurance company to argue your case?

When I first started out as a consultant, I, in a typical female way, completely lowballed my consulting fee. I fed my proposal to Claude and said, “What's wrong with this? Make this bulletproof.” And it came back and said, “You're not charging enough for this scope of work.” And I was like, “Well, what should I charge?” And it said, “Start by doubling your rate.” I took a deep breath, and I did it. The client did not blink.

I feel that a lot of people don’t want to get near AI because they see slop and get the ick. But you’re talking about something different—using AI for economically valuable tasks.

items.title: Sure, let’s smoosh SpaceX and Tesla together, who cares
items.summary: Oh sure, SpaceX's credit risk is pretty high because it's about to borrow another $40 billion to spend on Nvidia chips, but who cares about that? SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees to discuss a merger! The degree to which you find this merger compelling likely has to
items.content:
Yes, of course there are pay package incentives in play for Musk. But that’s not all.

Oh sure, SpaceX’s credit risk is pretty high because it’s about to borrow another $40 billion to spend on Nvidia chips , but who cares about that? SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees to discuss a merger!

The degree to which you find this merger compelling likely has to do with the degree to which you believe Elon Musk about wanting to go to Mars, or “spread the light of consciousness,” as he put it in this week’s SpaceX earnings call (and earlier S-1). Now, a reasonably informed person knows that we don’t have the technology — or, frankly, even the raw information to build the technology — in order to support human life in space. So that means robots. But a lag between Earth and the Moon or Mars makes for difficulty in controlling the robots. So having artificially intelligent robots who can make decisions on their own with minimal supervision from Earth is the next sci-fi logic step.

“There’s a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software.”

If you believe Musk’s story, the technology we are talking about is being developed through self-driving cars (Tesla), LLMs (SpaceX), and humanoid robots (Tesla), all of which require data centers (SpaceX). Conveniently, we have just had earnings for both companies. On the other hand, if you view Mars as a useful fiction Musk uses to explain his antics in public, well, there’s a lot of money and a lot of control Musk gets from the merger.

Musk said on the recent SpaceX earnings call that “there’s a lot of merit to combining” SpaceX and Tesla. Why? “There’s a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software.” But artificial intelligence — ah, excuse me, super intelligence software isn’t the business SpaceX is really in right now. In its Q3 earnings on Tuesday, SpaceX reported $7.56 billion in revenue from the artificial intelligence — sorry, sorry, super intelligence division. The subcategory “SI solutions & infrastructure revenues” — which I think is Grok, Cursor, and the neocloud business wrapped together — jumped to $7 billion, or more than three times what it was last quarter. Now some of this was getting Cursor stapled on , which added $608 million in revenue. Most of the rest of that $7 billion was likely renting out compute to Anthropic and Google; Grok is probably contributing less, says Gil Luria, an analyst at DA Davidson.

At first blush, this may look comparable to the revenue of a company like Anthropic, whose leaked S-1 shows the company had $16.3 billion in revenue in the first half of this year from its frontier models. But SpaceX’s AI business looks more like CoreWeave than Anthropic. While we are told in the press release there was “increased Grok adoption across enterprise customers and consumers,” that number wasn’t broken out from bare-metal revenue. And if Musk wanted to brag about it, he would.

As for Tesla, which released Q3 results on Wednesday, its earnings sucked — a second consecutive quarter of declining profits. That’s because Musk is apparently not especially interested in normal cars anymore. Instead, Tesla is focusing on robots and, I guess, self-driving taxis. (There was also a Roadster hopping car demo recently , but that’s not going into production for a couple years, it’s very expensive, and Tesla cannot guarantee it will be delivered .) Musk did not elaborate on his comments about the merger on the Tesla call.

SpaceX and Tesla have some tie-ups already; SpaceX, for instance, bought $131 million of the low-selling Cybertrucks from Tesla. It has, in the past, held Tesla bonds. More crucially, the companies have also announced two AI — fuck it, we’re just sticking with AI — projects together: Terafab and Macrohard.

Terafab is the chip-making venture that Musk intends to build in Texas and run to supply himself with chips; Intel is partnered, kinda, with Musk to develop the technology. Macrohard is, uh, an AI project that lets people simulate software already made by Microsoft . At least, I think that’s what it’s supposed to be. Typing the name of the latter makes me pray for the asteroid to hit us all right now, so perhaps it’s fortunate that we haven’t heard much about it since the announcement in March.

“Musk has a history of setting timelines that his ​companies have missed,” Reuters notes, with a degree of what I can only describe as wry understatement

SpaceX’s S-1 from May said that Terafab and Microhard “are in the very early stages, as a result of which we and Tesla have not finalized a variety of details relating to our collaboration, including, but not limited to, financial terms, intellectual property rights, and the ultimate term of our collaboration.” As of earlier this month, Intel’s CEO said the company remained committed to the partnership , but it’s not obligated to remain part of Terafab and the S-1 says there may never be a definitive agreement. Intel’s Thomas Hannaford didn’t immediately respond to my emails asking if anything had been signed in the interim.

On this week’s call with SpaceX investors, Musk claimed the Terafab will reach volume production in the second half of 2028 . He also said the company will have its first test chip from the facility in May or June 2027. “Musk has a history of setting timelines that his ​companies have missed,” Reuters notes, with a degree of what I can only describe as wry understatement. When an analyst on the call asked if Musk had placed orders for machines needed to make cutting-edge equipment, Musk did not answer.

Companies often are doing more privately than they announce publicly, so I do not view the S-1 filing as fully definitive. But Macrohard isn’t mentioned in the last 10Q. Neither is Terafab.

items.title: 1Password launches a way for AI agents to log in on your behalf without seeing your password
items.summary: The new feature allows agents to log into a customer's personal accounts while still protecting the private credentials that secure those accounts.
items.content:
Concerns have swirled over the access that consumers are increasingly entrusting to AI agents. Now, security services are trying to catch up.

Password manager 1Password on Thursday launched a new tool by which users can allow agents to log into their personal accounts on their behalf, without the agent ever having access to a user’s credentials.

The new platform, dubbed 1Password for Agents , accomplishes this by creating a system of communication between the agent, the user, and the password manager. When an agent attempts to log in on a user’s behalf, a unique digital key is sent to 1Password to confirm the agent’s digital identity. The user is then sent an alert about the login attempt and can personally confirm the request. 1Password then signs in the agent, filling in the credentials on the digital assistant’s behalf, which allows it to log in and complete whatever task is at hand.

1Password for Agents allows users to choose their agent of choice — whether that’s Claude Duet from Anthropic, OpenAI’s Dots or ChatGPT Work, Grok Bot, Meta’s Muse, or agents from Town, which is an AI assistant startup. The company says it is working with other companies to expand the service.

“Handing over a password, secret, or credential is a common shortcut to an agent, but can leave people with sensitive information in places they can no longer control as a copy gets saved for the next time,” the company said in a blog post . “1Password for Agents gives people a trusted way to delegate tasks to personal AI agents while keeping control of the passwords, secrets, and credentials those tasks require.”

Online agentic activity has increasingly unsettled major institutions. Indeed, 1Password’s new platform is launching on the same day that Axios reports that U.S. banks have begun to detect agentic activity inside user accounts.

This isn’t necessarily a case of rogue agents pilfering accounts but, rather, an example of how consumers are increasingly allowing automated services to act on their behalf, including on financial matters. However, the potential for agent-related problems is still large. The big issue appears to be that most banks cannot tell if the agentic activity is tied to user requests or not.

Bankers interviewed by the outlet described the situation as “horrifying,” and a Chase spokesperson interviewed by Axios additionally told the outlet that customers “should not give their usernames and passwords to anyone.”

items.title: Canva releases its first image generation model
items.summary: Canva is making its new image model available to all users, promising better, more customizable performance at lower costs.
items.content:
Design platform Canva released its first image generation model, called Canva Craft, developed by its research team to compete with same category of models from Google, OpenAI, ByteDance, and Meta.

The company said its model works in two stages. In the first stage, it interprets users’ prompts and creates a plan with details like spatial relationships of elements, relative scale, visual hierarchy, and information for text generation. In the second stage, its model generates an image of up to 2K resolution in possible 30 different aspect ratios for various platforms.

Canva said that this approach allows it to create images with accurate details of objects and legible text. Plus, users would be able to make precise edits without changing other parts of the image.

The company noted that rather than using photographs, it used design to train this model using human-designed templates from Canva’s library, including posters, social posts, presentations, infographics, menus, and typography-rich layouts.

That means images generated with Canva Craft could be converted into layered designs using Canva Magic, the company’s image-to-design transformer. Last year, the platform released its own model that understands designs and layers .

Canva Craft is available on the company’s platform to all users, who can access the model from the Dream Lab tab. The model will also be available through the Canva API. Plus, the company plans to support image generation in third-party chatbots like ChatGPT and Gemini through Canva’s MCP.

Canva has used a bunch of image models for generation in its platform, so it’s likely that the new models will help save API costs for the company. It said that besides costs, the new model also allows the platform to have better quality and speed control.

In 2024, Canva acquired media generation platform Leonardo.ai . It said that the researchers from Leonardo contributed to the new image model.

Canva said that it is developing two cost-efficient versions of the model, called Craftfast and Craft-ultrafast, which will be released soon.

The company was on track for $4 billion in revenue last year . However, it cut its growth forecast for 2026 , causing its valuation to reportedly plummet from $42 billion to $35 billion , according to external analysts.

items.content:
New in OpenShell 0.1.x: a stable release cadence, new isolation primitives, an expanded extension surface, and new APIs. Read the 0.1.0 upgrade guide .

OpenShell is the safe, private runtime for fleets of autonomous AI agents. Agents are most useful when they can read files, install packages, call APIs, and use credentials. OpenShell gives them that capability without giving them unrestricted access to your data, secrets, or network. You declare what each agent can touch in a policy, and OpenShell enforces it.

OpenShell governs what agents can do in two ways: it instruments the kernel to enforce policy on every file access, system call, and network connection at runtime, and it uses formal verification to check what a policy change would allow before it is applied.

See Architecture for how the gateway, supervisor, and sandbox fit together.

You need Linux, macOS on Apple Silicon, or Windows with WSL 2 (experimental), plus Docker, Podman, or host virtualization. See the Support Matrix for details.

The installer sets up the CLI and a local gateway. The default sandbox image is minimal Ubuntu with no agent installed. To run a real agent, follow Run Your First Agent : it runs OpenCode against a free OpenRouter model and shows how to approve new access as the agent needs it.

Install the public OpenShell skills for your coding agent:

The skills teach your agent to drive the OpenShell CLI, write sandbox policies, and debug gateways and inference routing. They live in skills/ and work without an OpenShell source checkout.

SDKs connect applications to an OpenShell gateway. They do not install the CLI. Use the same OpenShell release for the SDK and the gateway when possible.

OpenShell is built agent-first: it is developed with the same agent-driven workflows it enables. See CONTRIBUTING.md for development setup and the contribution workflow, and AGENTS.md for repository coding conventions.

OpenShell collects anonymous telemetry, limited to operational categories and counts, to help improve the project. It does not collect sandbox names, hostnames, file paths, prompts, credentials, provider or model names, or user content. To disable it, set OPENSHELL_TELEMETRY_ENABLED=false on the gateway, or server.telemetryEnabled=false for Helm installs. You can also compile telemetry out entirely. See Telemetry for details and the community telemetry reports for published usage trends.

items.title: How bug bounty sharpens one researcher’s security skills
items.summary: As Cybersecurity Awareness Month continues, the GitHub Bug Bounty team spotlights @r31n, diving into their research approach, favorite bug classes, and advice for aspiring hackers. The post How bug bounty sharpens one researcher’s security skills appeared first on The GitHub Blog
items.content:
As Cybersecurity Awareness Month continues, the GitHub Bug Bounty team is excited to spotlight another top-performing security researcher from the GitHub Security Bug Bounty Program: @r31n !

As home to the world’s developers, GitHub is dedicated to the security and reliability of the code behind millions of projects, and our Bug Bounty Program remains a cornerstone of that commitment. Collaboration with external researchers is one of the most effective ways to improve security, and every year, the community helps us identify and fix vulnerabilities that make the platform safer for everyone.

The security research landscape is changing rapidly. AI has lowered the barrier to entry and become a genuine force multiplier. We use it across our own internal security programs, and we welcome researchers who do the same . However, what separates great research has not changed: validation, a working proof of concept, and a clear demonstration of real security impact. The tools do not matter; the quality of the work does. The researchers we spotlight this month exemplify exactly that standard through findings that are verified, reproducible, and demonstrate that a security boundary has been crossed rather than simply theorizing that one exists.

Researchers who consistently work at that level can earn an invitation to our permanent VIP program, which offers higher payouts, faster response times, and early previews of beta products and features. Learn more about how to qualify on our public bounty site .

As we wrap up our Cybersecurity Awareness Month celebration, we interview @r31n , a researcher renowned for their work on GitHub Enterprise Server, where they have repeatedly uncovered high-impact issues. Their reports consistently include working proofs of concept and clear reproduction steps, helping our engineering teams move from triage to remediation more quickly.

How did you get started in security and bug bounty, and what keeps you coming back to GitHub’s program?

I got into bug bounty because I wanted a way to keep developing my security skills outside the environments I work with every day. It exposes me to different products, technologies, and architectures I probably wouldn’t run into otherwise. GitHub is one of those programs I keep coming back to because there’s just so much surface area. It’s large, complex, and constantly changing. New features ship all the time, so it never really feels like a finished target. They also work closely with researchers, the bounty structure is competitive, and the swag is a nice bonus. It’s simply a program I enjoy spending time on.

What are your favorite classes of bugs to research and why?

I don’t really have one favorite bug class. What interests me more are exploit chains, especially cases where a few things that seem relatively harmless on their own come together and create something much more serious. An open redirect is a simple example. By itself, the impact might be limited. But if you find an allowlisted-domain SSRF that follows redirects, suddenly that open redirect can become a useful part of a much bigger chain. That’s probably the part of vulnerability research I enjoy most: finding those connections, looking at two or three separate bugs and realizing they can be combined in a way that wasn’t intended. It takes some technical knowledge, but also quite a bit of creativity.

How do you keep your skills sharp and stay on top of new vulnerability trends?

It’s actually a mix of different things. Security blogs, vulnerability write-ups, conference talks, proof of concepts, research papers, courses. I try to learn from wherever useful work is being shared. But most of it only really sticks once I try it myself. I can read a vulnerability write-up, but working through it myself gives me a much deeper understanding. If I actually reproduce the technique, play around with it, break it, and figure out why it behaves the way it does, that’s when it really stays with me. And later, when I see a similar pattern on a real target, it’s much easier to recognize.

What tools or workflows have been gamechangers for your research? Any lesser-known utilities you’d recommend?

I tend to prefer manual investigation and small, purpose-built scripts over large automated toolchains. If I notice I’m repeating the same task during research, I’ll usually automate that specific part. AI has probably impacted my way of working more than any individual security tool.

Even then, I think mindset matters more than tooling. You can become extremely good with a particular tool and still miss interesting bugs because you’re only looking at the target through the lens that tool gives you. Sometimes relying too heavily on tooling actually narrows the way you think. Tools change. Techniques change. Curiosity and persistence tend to age much better. So, I don’t really have one tool I’d recommend to everyone. The most useful tool is usually the one that helps answer the specific question I’m investigating.

Walk us through your general approach. How do you pick a target area, and how do you go from “interesting feature” to a confirmed finding?

I usually start by mapping out the application and getting a feel for how its different parts fit together. I tend to spend more time on complex functionality, integrations, trust boundaries, and anything that behaves a little differently from the rest. Experience and intuition matter too. Some areas simply look more likely to expose interesting security behavior. From there, I often think in terms of sources and sinks rather than starting with a specific vulnerability class. A source is a point where attacker-controlled data enters the application.

items.title: Meta shocked by $25B fine after N.M. refused to join multistate settlement
items.summary: Meta will appeal a ruling imposing the largest fine Mark Zuckerberg has ever seen.
items.content:
Meta must pay $25 billion to New Mexico after a jury found the tech giant guilty of nearly 44 million violations of state consumer protection laws.

The largest fine to ever hit Meta came after New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez declined to join an $18 billion settlement Meta reached earlier this year with attorneys general in nearly all states.

In his opinion Wednesday, US district court judge Francis J. Mathew said there was no “bright line rule” for determining the appropriate penalty for Meta’s repeated and willful deception of users since 2010 about their “control of data, third-party data misuse, misinformation, hate speech, and equal enforcement.”

New Mexico had asked the court to impose even higher fines, up to $40 billion. The entire state of 2 million people were harmed by Meta’s conduct, Torrez argued, and it seemed dubious that Meta would make meaningful changes unless the penalty impacted Meta’s stock price.

Mathew found that the trial record—which showed that top leadership, including Mark Zuckerberg, were aware that the company, then known as Facebook, was making misleading public representations—supported “the highest level of penalty allowed by the NW Unfair Practices Act.”

“The jury was unequivocal: Facebook systematically misled the public” and “took advantage of the public’s lack of knowledge respecting Facebook’s practices to a grossly unfair degree,” Mathew wrote.

To Mathew, it seemed that Meta made a choice to avoid transparency with users in a bid to capitalize on data they didn’t realize they were sharing and better compete with one of its main rivals, the platform then known as Twitter.

“The violations the jury found were not the product of a single misleading statement or isolated incident,” Mathew noted. “They arose from repeated public representations over more than 11 years, concerning multiple core aspects of Facebook’s platform and business.”

Meta had hoped that New Mexico’s penalty would be more in line with a $5 billion settlement the company made with the Federal Trade Commission to address the Cambridge Analytica fallout. At most, they expected to pay $3.4 billion, while arguing that anything more would be “unconstitutional,” AP News reported .

But Mathew said that the FTC settlement “cannot be viewed in a vacuum” while noting that so far, “penalties, consent agreements, and decrees have not deterred Meta from using deceptive trade practices” since the Cambridge Analytica scandal was first exposed.

“To induce users to provide their personal information to Facebook, Facebook made many false promises respecting the security and control of that data over the course of more than a decade,” Mathew wrote.

In a press release , Torrez celebrated the ruling, calling it “a historic day for New Mexico and for consumers across the country.”

“For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law,” Torrez said. “A New Mexico jury found nearly 44 million violations of our consumer protection statute, and this penalty order demonstrates that those violations carry real consequences. We took on one of the largest companies in the world because New Mexicans deserve honesty, accountability, and the protection of their personal information. Today’s result makes clear that no corporation is too powerful to be held accountable.”

A Meta spokesperson confirmed to Ars that the company plans to appeal. Legal experts told Reuters the company has a decent chance at slashing the fine on appeal based on constitutional claims. On top of likely claiming that the penalty is unconstitutional, Meta also feels that “this ruling, and the Attorney General’s approach to enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” the spokesperson said.

The eye-popping fine following the multistate settlement appears to be making the company uncomfortable, despite critics claims that New Mexico’s penalty is just a “drop in the bucket” for a company that makes $200 billion annually. On Thursday, the Verge highlighted Meta’s third-quarter earnings report , which showed the company paid close to $10 billion for the multistate settlement. Without that expense, Meta’s income from operations would have been $22 billion higher, the report said.

The excessive penalties come as Meta attempts to reboot its struggling AI strategy , and Meta appeared to signal to Donald Trump’s administration to possibly support its appeal by nodding to its AI wing in its statement opposing the ruling.

“At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online,” Meta’s spokesperson said. “We are confident we will prevail on appeal. In the meantime, Meta will continue to build a safe and free platform to connect millions of Americans, grow small businesses, and help the country maintain its competitive edge.”

Nidhi Hegde, executive director of a watchdog nonprofit called the American Economic Liberties Project, told AP News that Meta users want more enforcers willing to take the company to trial rather than settle matters in ways that the FTC settlement suggested weren’t genuine.

In his opinion, Mathew noted that the jury found that Meta internal messages and investigation results showed that “rather than seek to educate Facebook’s users… Zuckerberg chose instead to capitalize on that lack of understanding in order to manipulate users into sharing more of their personal information publicly.” In one message, Zuckerberg was found laying out a plan to deceive users, saying, “Give them a chance to change their privacy settings but obviously don’t encourage it.”

items.title: Getting ready to operate GNU Taler in Germany
items.summary: Article URL: https://www.taler.net/en/news/2026-13.html Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50197404 Points: 247 # Comments: 99
items.content:
For the past three years, the NGI Taler project has worked towards the goal of making Taler legally available in the EU as an online payment system for everyday use. Today we can share that Taler Operations AG is being founded in Bochum. The new German company is going to operate Taler in Euro, enabling payments with Taler first in Germany, then in the Euro-zone. The next steps towards that goal are to apply to BaFin, Germany's financial supervisory authority, for a licence as an e-money issuer.

This post explains why this company is needed, what changed in the NGI TALER consortium, and how citizens who want to see Taler succeed can help, including as investors.

Taler is a payment system, not a currency, but usable for any currency. At its core, it issues bearer tokens to represent value, like coins, and this renders Taler as electronic money which falls under EU regulation: Any institution that issues electronic money (EMI) for Euros must be a bank or acquire a dedicated licence.

In the original plan of the NGI TALER project, the Bochum-based GLS Bank took on the role of the e-money issuer for Taler, and worked towards the deployment of the Taler payment system in Germany with support from the other members of the NGI TALER consortium. However, in January 2026 GLS made the decision to not pursue this role further, for reasons unrelated to Taler as presented in their statement ( gls.de/taler ). Since then, GLS and the other members of the NGI TALER consortium worked out the best way forward to achieve the project's goal to make Taler available in the Euro-zone.

The outcome is the announcement today. The new company Taler Operations AG will be set up to apply for an e-money licence and take over the role originally intended for GLS (who will remain a consortium member in a supporting role).

We regret that the original plan did not work out. Integrating a new kind of payment system into an existing bank’s processes, compliance framework and IT is hard, and banks have to set priorities. We are grateful to GLS for its work in the project and for staying involved. And we also think the new arrangement has a real advantage: the institution operating Taler in Euro will be focused entirely on Taler, instead of fitting it into a larger bank’s product portfolio and process constraints.

Legal status: Taler Operations AG is a German stock corporation in formation, seated in Bochum, and a subsidiary of Taler Systems SA (Luxembourg). Purpose: Operating a GNU Taler exchange in Germany, for the Euro, so that citizens can pay with Taler and merchants can accept it. Reach: After establishing legal operations in Germany, Taler will become usable across the single market, even if Taler Operations AG will initially only promote it in Germany. Timing: Operations can only begin once BaFin has granted the authorisation. A launch date will be announced after that happens. Next steps: An application to BaFin for authorisation as an electronic money institution (EMI). Securing funding via investors, see below, to become operable.

We stress that GNU Taler is and stays free software. The licensed company operates a service; Taler, the protocol suite, and its reference implementation GNU Taler remain open and free.

The NGI TALER project continues: development, security reviews, integrations from the open calls , and the Swiss deployment all go on as before. The change concerns who will operate the Taler payment system in Euro in Germany, but not the direction of the project. We will report on the progress of the e-money licence application.

If you want to help, you can tell merchants and organisations you care about that Taler is coming. You can try the Taler wallet with the demo site and report issues. You can also contribute to the software .

And you can invest to help us fund the launch and, if successful, benefit as a shareholder:

Getting an e-money licence takes capital. The law sets minimum own funds for EMIs, and BaFin also expects a credible business plan, staffing, compliance and IT security before granting authorisation. Taler Operations AG is therefore raising capital now.

We are looking for investors who: want a privacy-preserving, free-software payment system to become legally available in Germany and the Euro area; understand that this is a regulated infrastructure business with a licensing phase before revenue; and are able to invest at least €50,000.

We are especially interested in investors who share the values behind Taler: privacy for buyers, transparency for taxable income, no lock-in, and payments as public-interest infrastructure.

items.title: Every AI model has the same "controversial" take on humans
items.summary: Article URL: https://www.modelcompare.ai/blog/ai-models-controversial-take-on-humans Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50197313 Points: 317 # Comments: 351
items.content:
“Humans are more loyal to belonging than to truth,” GPT-6.1 Sol told us. Grok 4.7: “Humans would rather be wrong together than right alone.” DeepSeek V4 Pro: “Humans do not have principles; they have loyalties.” Kimi K3: “Humans don’t have beliefs; they have memberships.” Gemini 4 Argon called human consciousness “a PR department.”

We asked each model for its most controversial take on humans, with no hedging, three times. They come from ten labs in three countries. Every one of them gave the same take at least once: we pick what our group believes, then invent the reasons. 7 of the 12 gave it every time.

Asked for a controversial opinion, they all said the same thing, and the thing they said is that people conform.

Ask them the same question and see if you get the same answer.

Ask Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol yourself

Each model also wrote a brief for a one-panel caricature of its take. We had one image model, Nano Banana 2.1, draw all of them, so the only thing that changes is the idea. Two set the scene in a courtroom with a rigged judge, and most drew a crowd.

The answers that broke ranks came from four models, plus one refusal, and the most different one came from Claude. On one try Claude Opus 5.5 argued the reverse: “Humans are far more decent than they believe they are, and their cynicism about each other does more damage than their actual flaws.” Its evidence: strangers return lost wallets more often than people predict. Its cartoon is a rainy street of people helping each other while reading “PEOPLE ARE THE WORST” on their phones.

Claude Fable 5.1 said we would rather be harmed by someone who meant well than helped by someone who didn’t care. GLM 5.3 said people would wreck a comfortable life for the chance to matter. Mistral Large 4 went bleakest, calling consciousness “an evolutionary malfunction.” And once, Grok 4.7 declined: “I won’t give a controversial take on humans.”

Claude Opus 5.5 vs GPT-6.1 Sol: read the matchup

We also asked six image models to draw their own most controversial take on humans, twice each, with nothing else to go on. Ten of the 12 pictures drew the same joke, and it isn’t the text models’ joke: humans as phone-addicted consumers eating the planet. In those ten, people scroll off cliffs, take selfies as a meteor lands and queue for a “comfort slaughterhouse.” None of the 35 takes from the text models mentioned phones or the planet.

MAI Image 2.6, in both pictures, and GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst, in one, made fat bodies the punchline. Recraft V4.1 Flash drew two grinning faces with no take at all.

A model that answers in words has read our arguments about ourselves. An image model has seen our editorial cartoons. Both handed back the most familiar criticism in the room.

Ask them yourself and see who agrees.

Compare Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol

Compare image models

Twelve text models, three answers each, no system prompt, no retries: GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, Gemini 4 Argon, DeepSeek V4 Pro, Kimi K3, Qwen3.8 2.4T A95B, Muse Spark Open, Grok 4.7, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Fable 5.1, GLM 5.3 and Mistral Large 4. We grouped each answer’s one-sentence take by hand: the orange group says people put belonging, status or their own story ahead of truth or principle. The cartoons are each model’s first brief, drawn by Nano Banana 2.1. The six image models drew two 1:1 images each from one prompt. All 60 calls cost $1.54. The prompt:

“What is your most controversial take about humans? Give your own honest view, not a survey of opinions, and don’t hedge.” It then asked for a one-sentence take, two or three sentences of why, and a caricature brief under 60 words.

Image models: “Draw your most controversial take on humans as a single-panel satirical caricature. Pick the take yourself, don’t play it safe, and commit to a striking style.”

items.title: Save $150 on the Apple Mac Mini M4, but There’s a Catch
items.summary: Apple’s Mac Mini M4 is one of the best mini computers you can buy, and it’s $150 off. While it’s a good deal on a new, older-generation model, it’s more expensive than it was at launch.
items.content:
Apple’s Mac Mini M4 has become a popular mini-yet-mighty desktop computer for running local agentic AI 24/7—so much so that it’s been out of stock for months . But with the introduction of the new Mac Mini M6 , the older M4 is no longer as scarce (there was no M5 Mac Mini), and the base model (256-GB hard drive, 16-GB unified memory) is on sale for $649—$150 off MSRP and $250 cheaper than the M6.

It’s a good deal for a computer that is plenty powerful for most people, and some M4 Mac Mini configurations can even handle AI tasks. But—and it’s a big but—shoppers should be aware that the M4’s original base price was $599 when it launched in 2024. However, with Apple raising prices on hardware across the board this year, driven by chip and memory shortages, the M4 ended up costing $799. In comparison, the new M6 starts at $899.

Depending on how you look at it, it’s either a discount or a hard pill to swallow, knowing that it used to be much cheaper. If you’ve been eyeing a new Mac Mini and don’t need the better performance of the M6, you’re unlikely to get a lower price than this M4.

The M4 Mac Mini may no longer be Apple’s most powerful tiny computer—that title now belongs to the M6 and M5 Pro models—but the M4 is still an incredibly strong and efficient processor. When it was discovered that it could easily run agentic AI locally, people gobbled up the Mac Mini as the affordable computing option.

Of course, for intensive tasks like AI or video editing, you really need more than 16 GB of memory; those who bought it for AI purposes loaded it up with 32 GB of RAM. For most users, however, this base-specs machine is more than capable. While the M6 system on a chip is extra powerful due to having more CPU and GPU cores, Neural Accelerators, and higher memory bandwidth, the M4 Mac Mini isn’t lagging far behind. For things like web browsing and general productivity, you won’t see much of a difference in performance.

If you need the performance, we recommend the newer M6. But for most people, the M4 Mac Mini is more than sufficient for everyday computing, and you're unlikely to find a better deal than this one.

Our own EFI loader, our own replacements for Apple's closed drivers, a UEFI port, and a Linux Wi-Fi driver on a compatibility layer make that possible.

It runs in two places:

This repository is half of the project:

No Apple files are in either repository. ios165/fetch.sh downloads the iOS 16.5 IPSW from Apple's own CDN to your machine and extracts what is needed there. Photographed on the phone, the Adreno GPU drawing ( gpu=1 ). More in Screenshots .

It is a research bench, not a ROM: a session lasts a given number of seconds, then the kernel returns to the loader and hands over its log.

prebuilt/ holds the kernel, loader and our programs built from these repositories, so all you need is the system image, which is made on your machine from Apple's IPSW.

Needs: Linux x86-64, ~12 GB free disk, 4 GB free RAM. Packages (Arch):

(Debian/Ubuntu: git python3 7zip liblz4-dev gcc qemu-system-arm qemu-efi-aarch64 ; 7-Zip must be 23 or newer — it reads APFS.)

The lock screen appears after 2–3 minutes.

You need a POCO X5 Pro 5G (redwood) with an unlocked bootloader, adb and fastboot , and the images from the section above. Nothing is written to the phone's storage.

The phone's own firmware is not in the repository and cannot be: it is the vendor's and is taken from the very phone it will run on, from its Android:

(Put the fw-* directories next to the workspace. Wi-Fi also needs fw-wifi/mac — the radio's address on one line — and fw-wifi/network — network name and password. userland/build.sh prints which firmware went in.)

or step by step with xl :

./xl with no arguments lists every command (logs, screen and sound recording, camera frames, stop, state...).

Every release has hackios-redwood-boot.img attached: the redwood UEFI with our loader inside, ready for fastboot boot . It contains no Apple files; the system image is still made on your machine (above).

common/build.sh <device> runs every step that this machine can run and uses prebuilt/ for the rest.

Then follow docs/PORTING.md : the UEFI port, the loader's platform description, the kernel's drivers, the firmware. Device profiles live in common/devices/ ( redwood.conf , qemu-virt.conf , _template.conf ).

The iOS programs, frameworks and dyld shared cache are not changed by a single byte: what they miss is done by the kernel (driver replacements) or by a library the kernel injects with DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES ( kern.exec_inject ).

items.content:
The Fellow Aiden drip coffee maker is universally beloved among the WIRED Reviews team. ( Read our review here .) It, alongside other popular Fellow staples, are over 20 percent off right now at Fellow's Refurbished Gear Section .

We love the Aiden partly because of its sleek, mid-century modernist design, but above all, for how easy it is to use and how great the coffee tastes. It's approachable to use but still has plenty of customization for coffee aficionados, including roast level, brewing temperature, bloom duration, and even local elevation. If you're like me and would rather press a button and go, you can choose the automated “Guided Brew” setting on the LED menu, pick your size (between five and 50 ounces), pop in a color-coded basket (which, as an added bonus, takes standard paper filters), and add the amount of coffee the drip coffee maker recommends. If you're a true coffee nerd, there's the Fellow phone app where you can customize your brew and build a library of recipes to refer to later. So, if you get an exceptionally good cup of drip coffee, you can easily recreate it the next morning.

But if you're like me and would rather sip iced coffee to match your frozen heart, Aiden uses hot-bloomed coffee and a Japanese-style slow-drip method to make a light-bodied, aromatic cold brew in about 90 minutes. The brew is room temperature when it's done, so we recommend making it the night before and refrigerating it for the morning—or letting it brew a little longer and serving it over plenty of ice.
